bmt-2019-power-01.title: Induction
bmt-2019-power-01.body: For $n=1$: $1=\frac{1\cdot3\cdot2}6$. Suppose the formula holds for $n=k$. Then $\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}i^2=\frac{k(2k+1)(k+1)}6+(k+1)^2=\frac{(k+1)\left[k(2k+1)+6(k+1)\right]}6=\frac{(k+1)(2k^2+7k+6)}6=\frac{(k+1)(k+2)(2k+3)}6$, which is the formula for $n=k+1$. ∎

bmt-2019-power-03a.title: Use a prime
bmt-2019-power-03a.body: Take any prime $p$. Then $D(p)=D(1\cdot p)=1\cdot D(p)+p\,D(1)=D(p)+pD(1)$, so $pD(1)=0$ and $D(1)=0$. ∎

bmt-2019-power-03b.title: Induction
bmt-2019-power-03b.body: For $k=0$, $D(1)=0=0\cdot p^{-1}$ by the previous part. Let $k\ge1$ and suppose $D(p^{k-1})=(k-1)p^{k-2}$ (for $k=1$ this says $D(1)=0$). Then $D(p^k)=pD(p^{k-1})+p^{k-1}D(p)=p(k-1)p^{k-2}+p^{k-1}=kp^{k-1}$. ∎

bmt-2019-power-05.title: Induction
bmt-2019-power-05.body: Write $n=q_1q_2\cdots q_t$ with primes $q_i$ (repeats allowed); then the claim is $D(n)=n\sum_{i=1}^t\frac1{q_i}$ (grouping equal primes gives $\sum e_i/p_i$). For $t=0$, $n=1$ and $D(1)=0$ is the empty sum. If it holds for $n=q_1\cdots q_{t}$, then for $n'=nq_{t+1}$: $D(n')=q_{t+1}D(n)+nD(q_{t+1})=q_{t+1}n\sum_{i\le t}\frac1{q_i}+n=nq_{t+1}\left(\sum_{i\le t}\frac1{q_i}+\frac1{q_{t+1}}\right)=n'\sum_{i\le t+1}\frac1{q_i}$. ∎

bmt-2019-power-06d.title: Use the exponent formula
bmt-2019-power-06d.body: If $n=\prod p_i^{e_i}$ then $n^k=\prod p_i^{ke_i}$, so $D(n^k)=n^k\sum\frac{ke_i}{p_i}=k\,n^{k-1}\cdot n\sum\frac{e_i}{p_i}=k\,n^{k-1}D(n)$ (for $n=1$ both sides are $0$). ∎

bmt-2019-power-07.title: Contrapositive
bmt-2019-power-07.body: We show: if Goldbach is true, then for every $k>1$ some $n$ has $D(n)=2k$. Since $2k>2$ is even, there are primes $p,q$ with $p+q=2k$. For $n=pq$, $D(n)=pD(q)+qD(p)=p+q=2k$ (this also holds when $p=q$, as $D(p^2)=2p$). Hence if no $n$ has $D(n)=2k$ for some $k>1$, Goldbach fails for $2k$. ∎

bmt-2019-power-09b.title: Divisibility argument
bmt-2019-power-09b.body:
Let $D(n)=n$ with $n>1$ (note $D(1)=0
e1$) and $n=p_1^{e_1}\cdots p_k^{e_k}$. Then $\sum_{i=1}^k rac{e_i}{p_i}=1$. Multiply by $P=p_1\cdots p_k$: $\sum_{i=1}^ke_i\prod_{j
e i}p_j=P$. Fix $i$ and reduce modulo $p_i$: every term with index $
e i$ contains the factor $p_i$, and so does $P$, hence $e_i\prod_{j
e i}p_j\equiv0\pmod{p_i}$. The $p_j$ ($j
e i$) are different primes, so $p_i\mid e_i$, hence $e_i\ge p_i$ and $ rac{e_i}{p_i}\ge1$ for every $i$. The sum of the $k$ terms equals $1$, so $k=1$ and $e_1=p_1$: $n=p_1^{p_1}$. With part (a), these are exactly the solutions. ∎

bmt-2019-power-10a.title: Compute
bmt-2019-power-10a.body:
$\Delta(12)=16,32,80,176,368,\dots$: $D(12)=16$, $D(16)=32$, $D(32)=80$, $D(80)=176$, and every term is divisible by $4$ with $D(a)\ge a$ for such $a$ (see part (d)), so the sequence is increasing.

**Answer: increasing**

bmt-2019-power-10c.title: An example
bmt-2019-power-10c.body: Take $n=26$. $D(26)=26\left(\frac12+\frac1{13}\right)=15$, $D(15)=15\left(\frac13+\frac15\right)=8$, $D(8)=12$. So $\Delta(26)$ begins $15,8,12,\dots$: the first step decreases ($15>8$, so not increasing) and the second step increases ($8<12$, so not decreasing). Hence $\Delta(26)$ is neither. ∎

bmt-2019-power-10d.title: Terms divisible by 4
bmt-2019-power-10d.body:
Let $a=4c$ ($c\ge1$). Then $D(a)=cD(4)+4D(c)=4c+4D(c)=4(c+D(c))\ge a$, and $D(a)$ is again divisible by $4$. If $k\ge2$, $2^k$ is divisible by $4$, hence so is $D(2^k)=k2^{k-1}$ (for $k=2$ it is $4$, for $k\ge3$ it has the factor $2^{k-1}\ge4$). By induction every term of $\Delta(2^k)$ is divisible by $4$ and each term is at most the next one: increasing.

For $k=1$: $\Delta(2)=1,0,0,\dots$ is decreasing, not increasing. For $k=0$: $D(1)=0$ and the sequence is $0,0,\dots$, which is (trivially) increasing; this case was not intended by the problem. So the sequence is increasing exactly for $k\ge2$ (and the degenerate $k=0$). ∎

bmt-2019-power-11.title: Factor out $p^p$
bmt-2019-power-11.body: For any $c\ge1$, $D(c\,p^p)=cD(p^p)+p^pD(c)=(c+D(c))p^p$ since $D(p^p)=p^p$. Starting from $n=kp^p$ with $c_0=k>1$, define $c_{j+1}=c_j+D(c_j)$. Then $D^{(j)}(n)=c_jp^p$ for all $j\ge1$ by induction. Since $c_j\ge2$ we have $D(c_j)\ge1$ (as $D(c)=c\sum e_i/p_i>0$ for $c\ge2$), so $c_{j+1}>c_j$ and the sequence is strictly increasing. ∎

bmt-2019-power-12.title: A lemma on p-adic valuations
bmt-2019-power-12.body:
Write $x$ for either number and $y=D(x)$ for the other, so $D(m)=n'$ and $D(n')=m$.

**Lemma.** If $x=p^ar$ with $p\nmid r$ and $a\ge1$, then $D(x)=p^{a-1}(ar+pD(r))$. So if $p\nmid a$ then $v_p(D(x))=a-1$ exactly (because $p\nmid ar$).

**Step 1: $p^p\nmid m,n'$.** If $n'=kp^p$: for $k=1$, $D(n')=n'$ so $m=n'$, a contradiction. For $k>1$, as in problem 11, $m=D(n')=(k+D(k))p^p$ with $g=k+D(k)>k>1$, and then $n'=D(m)=(g+D(g))p^p>m>n'$, a contradiction. Likewise for $m$.

**Step 2: $\gcd(m,n')=1$.** Suppose a prime $p$ divides both, with $a=v_p(n')\ge1$ and $b=v_p(m)\ge1$. By Step 1, $a,b\le p-1$, so $p\nmid a$ and $p\nmid b$. The lemma gives $b=v_p(D(n'))=a-1$ and $a=v_p(D(m))=b-1$, so $b=a-1=b-2$, impossible.

**Step 3: squarefree.** Suppose $p^2\mid n'$ and let $a=v_p(n')\ge2$. By Step 1, $a\le p-1$ (so $p\ge3$ and $p\nmid a$), and the lemma gives $v_p(m)=a-1\ge1$. Then $p$ divides both $m$ and $n'$, contradicting Step 2. By symmetry, $m$ is squarefree too. ∎

bmt-2019-power-13.title: Bound each term
bmt-2019-power-13.body: Write $n=q_1q_2\cdots q_k$ with primes $q_i\ge p^*$ (repeats allowed). Then $D(n)=n\sum_{i=1}^k\frac1{q_i}\le\frac{nk}{p^*}$. Since $n\ge(p^*)^k$, $k\le\log_{p^*}n$, so $D(n)\le\frac{n\log_{p^*}(n)}{p^*}$. ∎

bmt-2019-power-14.title: AM-GM
bmt-2019-power-14.body: Write $n=q_1\cdots q_k$ (primes, repeats allowed). Then $\frac{D(n)}n=\sum_{i=1}^k\frac1{q_i}\ge k\left(\prod\frac1{q_i}\right)^{1/k}=k\,n^{-1/k}$ by AM-GM. So $D(n)\ge k\,n^{1-1/k}$. ∎

bmt-2019-power-15.title: Cases
bmt-2019-power-15.body:
If $k=1$, $n$ is prime and $D(n)=1=\frac{0}{2}n+2^0$. Let $k>1$ and write $n=q_1\cdots q_k$ with primes $q_i$, so $D(n)=n\sum\frac1{q_i}$.

**At least three factors $\ge3$.** Each such factor contributes at most $\frac13$ and every other factor at most $\frac12$, so $\sum\frac1{q_i}\le\frac{k-3}2+1\le\frac{k-1}2$, and $D(n)\le\frac{k-1}2n\le\frac{k-1}2n+2^{k-1}$.

**At most one factor $\ge3$.** Then $n=2^{k-1}q$ for a prime $q$ (possibly $q=2$), and $D(n)=n\left(\frac{k-1}2+\frac1q\right)=\frac{k-1}2n+\frac n q=\frac{k-1}2n+2^{k-1}$.

**Exactly two factors $\ge3$**, say $q_1,q_2$. Then $n=2^{k-2}q_1q_2$ and $D(n)=n\left(\frac{k-2}2+\frac1{q_1}+\frac1{q_2}\right)$. Since $q_1,q_2\ge3$, $(q_1-2)(q_2-2)=q_1q_2-2q_1-2q_2+4\ge0$; dividing by $q_1q_2$ gives $\frac1{q_1}+\frac1{q_2}\le\frac12+\frac2{q_1q_2}$. Hence $D(n)\le n\frac{k-1}2+\frac{2n}{q_1q_2}=\frac{k-1}2n+2\cdot2^{k-2}=\frac{k-1}2n+2^{k-1}$.

These cases cover all $n$. ∎
